findings.evidence: This recommendation applies to items returned within 60 days of their due date; items still unreturned past that window remain subject to the existing replacement-cost billing process, matching the return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established.
findings.fix: Either report the pilot's return-timing distribution (for example, what share of eventual returns occurred within 60 days) so the 60-day threshold is checkable against actual data, or drop the claim that the window matches an established pilot pattern and state the 60-day figure as an operational choice instead.
findings.violation: TOULMIN-GROUNDS: the 60-day cutoff is justified by appeal to a return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established, but the pilot results reported in What the Pilot Showed give only a single aggregate on-time-or-eventual rate (94 percent versus 87 percent) and a survey percentage; no day-by-day or time-windowed return pattern is reported anywhere in the artifact for a reader to check against the 60-day figure.

findings.evidence: A skeptic on the board points to overdue fines as a source of materials-replacement funding... Consortium finance records show fine revenue covered under 2 percent of the annual materials budget over the last three fiscal years, and the four pilot branches absorbed the loss without a measurable change to their replacement-copy spending.
findings.fix: Add a paragraph addressing materials availability and hold-queue wait times under the no-fine policy, using whatever hold-fulfillment or turnaround data the pilot branches already track, the same way the revenue objection is answered with finance data.
findings.location: Addressing the Revenue Concern section (lines 29 to 33)
findings.violation: TOULMIN-REBUTTAL: the artifact raises and answers the revenue objection, but its own grounds expose a second, un-raised risk it never addresses: What the Pilot Showed reports a combined on-time-or-eventual return rate, meaning items can still come back late without a fine, and the artifact never considers or rebuts the risk that removing the penalty lengthens how long patrons who are not returning on time hold items, reducing availability for other patrons waiting on holds.
